questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.topic: Lower limb: femoral/sciatic nerve, foot drop
questions.stem: Which nerve is at risk during an intramuscular injection given in the lower medial quadrant of the buttock, and what deficit results?
options: The sciatic nerve, causing foot drop with loss of sensation over the sole and lateral leg
The femoral nerve, causing loss of knee extension
The obturator nerve, causing loss of adduction
The pudendal nerve, causing incontinence
questions.concept: Injections are given in the upper outer quadrant precisely to avoid the nerve, and the resulting palsy affects the common peroneal component most because its fascicles lie laterally and are more vulnerable.
questions.reference: Snell Clinical Anatomy by Regions 10e, Ch. The Lower Limb

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.topic: Lower limb: femoral/sciatic nerve, foot drop
questions.stem: A patient cannot evert the foot but dorsiflexion is preserved, with sensory loss over the lower lateral leg and dorsum. Which nerve is injured?
options: The superficial peroneal nerve
The deep peroneal nerve
The tibial nerve
The sural nerve
questions.concept: The deep division supplies the dorsiflexors and a small web-space patch of skin, so isolated loss of eversion with preserved dorsiflexion localises the lesion to the superficial division rather than to the common trunk.
questions.reference: Snell Clinical Anatomy by Regions 10e, Ch. The Lower Limb

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.topic: Lower limb: femoral/sciatic nerve, foot drop
questions.stem: Which artery is the chief supply to the head of the femur in an adult, and why does a fracture of the femoral neck threaten it?
options: The medial circumflex femoral artery through its retinacular branches, which run along the neck and are torn by a displaced intracapsular fracture
The obturator artery through the ligamentum teres, which is the main supply in adults
The lateral circumflex femoral artery
The first perforating branch of the profunda femoris
questions.concept: The artery of the ligamentum teres contributes significantly only in childhood, which is why avascular necrosis follows a displaced intracapsular fracture in an adult and internal fixation is often replaced by arthroplasty.
questions.reference: Snell Clinical Anatomy by Regions 10e, Ch. The Lower Limb

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.topic: Lower limb: femoral/sciatic nerve, foot drop
questions.stem: Which structures pass through the adductor canal, and what is its surgical importance?
options: The femoral artery and vein with the nerve to vastus medialis and the saphenous nerve, making it the site of femoral artery exposure in the thigh
The sciatic nerve and popliteal vessels
The obturator nerve and vessels
The great saphenous vein alone
questions.concept: The canal ends at the adductor hiatus where the vessels become the popliteal artery and vein, and blockade of the saphenous nerve here provides analgesia for knee surgery while sparing quadriceps power.
questions.reference: Snell Clinical Anatomy by Regions 10e, Ch. The Lower Limb

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.topic: Lower limb: femoral/sciatic nerve, foot drop
questions.stem: A patient walks with the trunk lurching towards the affected side and a positive Trendelenburg sign after hip surgery. Which nerve and muscles are affected?
options: The superior gluteal nerve supplying gluteus medius and minimus, the abductors that stabilise the pelvis in single-leg stance
The inferior gluteal nerve supplying gluteus maximus
The femoral nerve supplying quadriceps
The obturator nerve supplying adductors
questions.concept: The lurch shifts the centre of gravity over the affected hip to reduce the abductor moment required, which is why the compensation itself is diagnostic of abductor weakness rather than of pain.
questions.reference: Snell Clinical Anatomy by Regions 10e, Ch. The Lower Limb

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.topic: Abdomen: peritoneum, liver & biliary, portal system
questions.stem: Which peritoneal recess is the commonest site of a subphrenic collection after upper abdominal surgery, and why?
options: The right subphrenic and subhepatic spaces, because peritoneal fluid is drawn upward along the right paracolic gutter by the negative pressure of respiration
The left paracolic gutter, because it is deeper
The lesser sac, because it is closed
The pelvic cavity, which never collects fluid
questions.concept: The phrenicocolic ligament limits upward spread on the left, so a right-sided collection with referred shoulder pain and a pleural effusion is the classic postoperative presentation.
questions.reference: Snell Clinical Anatomy by Regions 10e, Ch. The Abdomen

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.topic: Abdomen: peritoneum, liver & biliary, portal system
questions.stem: Which segments of the liver are removed in a right hepatectomy, and what defines the plane of resection?
options: Segments 5 to 8, with the plane defined by the middle hepatic vein and the line of Cantlie rather than by the falciform ligament
Segments 2 to 4, with the plane at the falciform ligament
Segments 1 to 4
Segments 4 to 8, with the plane at the right hepatic vein
questions.concept: The Couinaud scheme divides the liver by the portal and hepatic venous anatomy, and this functional rather than surface anatomy is what makes segmental and lobar resection possible.
questions.reference: Snell Clinical Anatomy by Regions 10e, Ch. The Abdomen

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.topic: Abdomen: peritoneum, liver & biliary, portal system
questions.stem: Which anatomical variant of the cystic artery most often causes bleeding during laparoscopic cholecystectomy?
options: A cystic artery arising from the right hepatic artery but crossing anterior to the bile duct or arising outside Calot triangle
A cystic artery arising from the portal vein
Absence of the cystic artery
A cystic artery arising from the splenic artery
questions.concept: A right hepatic artery running a tortuous course close to the cystic duct, the caterpillar hump, is the other classic hazard, which is why the critical view of safety is established before any structure is divided.
questions.reference: Snell Clinical Anatomy by Regions 10e, Ch. The Abdomen

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.topic: Brachial plexus & nerve injuries (radial/median/ulnar)
questions.stem: A patient has clawing of the ring and little fingers with a positive Froment sign and normal sensation over the dorsum of the hand. Where is the lesion?
options: The ulnar nerve at the wrist, distal to the origin of the dorsal cutaneous branch
The ulnar nerve at the elbow
The median nerve at the wrist
The lower brachial plexus
questions.concept: The dorsal cutaneous branch leaves about 5 cm proximal to the wrist, so preserved dorsal sensation with motor loss localises the injury distally, and the thumb adductor weakness compensated by flexor pollicis longus is what the Froment sign demonstrates.
questions.reference: Snell Clinical Anatomy by Regions 10e, Ch. The Upper Limb

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.topic: Brachial plexus & nerve injuries (radial/median/ulnar)
questions.stem: A patient has weakness of shoulder abduction and elbow flexion with a small pupil and drooping eyelid on the same side after a motorcycle crash. What does the pupillary sign indicate?
options: Avulsion of the T1 root proximal to the sympathetic outflow, indicating a preganglionic injury with a poor prognosis for recovery
Injury to the axillary nerve
A postganglionic rupture with a good prognosis
Injury to the long thoracic nerve
questions.concept: An associated Horner syndrome, elevated hemidiaphragm or winged scapula all point to root avulsion rather than a distal rupture, which changes management from expectant to early nerve transfer surgery.
questions.reference: Snell Clinical Anatomy by Regions 10e, Ch. The Upper Limb

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.topic: Cerebrum: blood supply, internal capsule, basal ganglia, cerebellum
questions.stem: Occlusion of which artery causes weakness of the contralateral leg greater than the arm with urinary incontinence?
options: The anterior cerebral artery, supplying the medial surface including the paracentral lobule
The middle cerebral artery
The posterior cerebral artery
The basilar artery
questions.concept: The leg area lies on the medial surface within the territory of this vessel, and bilateral involvement from an anterior communicating artery aneurysm can produce paraplegia with abulia and a grasp reflex.
questions.reference: Snell Clinical Anatomy by Regions 10e, Ch. The Head and Neck

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.topic: Cerebrum: blood supply, internal capsule, basal ganglia, cerebellum
questions.stem: Occlusion of the posterior cerebral artery produces which visual defect, and why is central vision often spared?
options: Contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing, because the occipital pole receives collateral supply from the middle cerebral artery
Bitemporal hemianopia, because the chiasma is supplied by this vessel
Monocular blindness
Upper quadrantanopia only
questions.concept: The same vessel supplies the thalamus and midbrain, so an infarct may be accompanied by hemisensory loss, a third nerve palsy or memory disturbance from medial temporal involvement.
questions.reference: Snell Clinical Anatomy by Regions 10e, Ch. The Head and Neck

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.topic: Cerebrum: blood supply, internal capsule, basal ganglia, cerebellum
questions.stem: A lesion of which cerebellar structure causes truncal ataxia with a wide-based gait and little limb incoordination?
options: The vermis and flocculonodular lobe, which is the midline vestibulocerebellum and spinocerebellum
The lateral hemisphere, which causes truncal ataxia
The dentate nucleus
The superior cerebellar peduncle
questions.concept: Medulloblastoma in a child arises in this midline region, whereas a lateral hemispheric lesion instead causes ipsilateral limb dysmetria, intention tremor and dysdiadochokinesia.
questions.reference: Snell Clinical Anatomy by Regions 10e, Ch. The Head and Neck

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.topic: General embryology & histology: fertilisation, placenta, epithelia
questions.stem: Which structure gives rise to the amnion, and what is the consequence of oligohydramnios in the second trimester?
options: The epiblast, and severe oligohydramnios causes Potter sequence with pulmonary hypoplasia, limb deformity and a flattened facies
The trophoblast, and oligohydramnios causes hydrops
The hypoblast, and oligohydramnios has no effect
The extraembryonic mesoderm, and oligohydramnios causes polyhydramnios
questions.concept: Amniotic fluid is largely fetal urine after the first trimester, so bilateral renal agenesis or obstruction produces the sequence and the lethal element is the failure of lung development.
questions.reference: Langman Medical Embryology 14e, Ch. Gametogenesis and First Weeks

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.topic: General embryology & histology: fertilisation, placenta, epithelia
questions.stem: Which type of epithelium lines the urinary bladder, and what is its functional advantage?
options: Transitional epithelium or urothelium, which allows distension without loss of the barrier
Simple columnar epithelium, which allows absorption
Keratinised stratified squamous epithelium, which resists abrasion
Simple cuboidal epithelium, which allows secretion
questions.concept: The umbrella cells with their specialised plaques and tight junctions maintain the barrier against urine as the surface area changes, and it is this epithelium that gives rise to the commonest bladder carcinoma.
questions.reference: Langman Medical Embryology 14e, Ch. Gametogenesis and First Weeks

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.topic: General embryology & histology: fertilisation, placenta, epithelia
questions.stem: Which germ layer gives rise to the adrenal medulla, and what does this explain clinically?
options: Neural crest ectoderm, which explains why phaeochromocytoma arises with other neural crest tumours in the multiple endocrine neoplasia syndromes
Mesoderm, the same as the cortex
Endoderm, the same as the thyroid
Surface ectoderm
questions.concept: The cortex derives from intermediate mesoderm instead, so a single gland has two embryologically distinct halves, and extra-adrenal chromaffin tissue along the sympathetic chain explains paragangliomas outside the gland.
questions.reference: Langman Medical Embryology 14e, Ch. Gametogenesis and First Weeks

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.topic: Head & neck: triangles, thyroid, parotid, TMJ
questions.stem: Which nerve is at risk during ligation of the inferior thyroid artery, and what is the resulting deficit?
options: The recurrent laryngeal nerve, causing hoarseness with a paramedian vocal cord
The external laryngeal nerve, causing loss of high notes
The hypoglossal nerve, causing tongue deviation
The glossopharyngeal nerve, causing loss of gag
questions.concept: The artery is therefore ligated well away from the gland close to its origin, whereas the superior thyroid artery is ligated close to the gland to protect the external laryngeal nerve, so the two vessels follow opposite rules.
questions.reference: Snell Clinical Anatomy by Regions 10e, Ch. The Head and Neck

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.topic: Head & neck: triangles, thyroid, parotid, TMJ
questions.stem: Which structure lies immediately deep to the submandibular gland and is at risk during its excision?
options: The lingual nerve, the hypoglossal nerve and the facial artery
The internal carotid artery
The glossopharyngeal nerve
The vagus nerve in the carotid sheath
questions.concept: The marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve is also at risk in the skin incision, which is why the incision is placed two finger-breadths below the mandible.
questions.reference: Snell Clinical Anatomy by Regions 10e, Ch. The Head and Neck

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.topic: Head & neck: triangles, thyroid, parotid, TMJ
questions.stem: Which anatomical feature of the temporomandibular joint permits the wide opening of the mouth, and which movement causes anterior dislocation?
options: Translation of the condyle forward onto the articular eminence during the second phase of opening, so excessive opening can carry it anterior to the eminence
A purely hinge movement at the condyle
Rotation of the disc alone
Posterior translation of the condyle
questions.concept: Reduction requires downward and backward pressure on the molars to lift the condyle back over the eminence, and recurrent dislocation is associated with joint laxity and a shallow eminence.
questions.reference: Snell Clinical Anatomy by Regions 10e, Ch. The Head and Neck

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.topic: Pelvis & perineum: pelvic floor, urogenital triangle
questions.stem: Which nerve block is used for the second stage of labour and forceps delivery, and where is the landmark?
options: Pudendal nerve block at the ischial spine, approached transvaginally
Obturator nerve block at the obturator foramen
Paracervical block at the uterosacral ligament
Ilioinguinal nerve block at the anterior superior iliac spine
questions.concept: The nerve leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen and re-enters through the lesser, hooking around the spine, and it supplies the perineal skin, external anal sphincter and the anal canal below the pectinate line.
questions.reference: Snell Clinical Anatomy by Regions 10e, Ch. The Pelvis and Perineum

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.topic: Pelvis & perineum: pelvic floor, urogenital triangle
questions.stem: Which fascial arrangement determines the pattern of urine extravasation after rupture of the membranous urethra?
options: Rupture above the perineal membrane allows urine to extravasate into the extraperitoneal pelvic tissue around the bladder rather than into the superficial perineal pouch
Urine always tracks into the scrotum and anterior abdominal wall
Urine enters the peritoneal cavity
Urine tracks into the ischioanal fossa
questions.concept: Bulbar urethral rupture below the membrane instead fills the superficial pouch and spreads into the scrotum, penis and anterior abdominal wall, so the site of injury is inferred from where the swelling appears.
questions.reference: Snell Clinical Anatomy by Regions 10e, Ch. The Pelvis and Perineum

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.topic: Pelvis & perineum: pelvic floor, urogenital triangle
questions.stem: Which structure must be preserved to maintain continence during a low anterior resection for rectal carcinoma?
options: The puborectalis component of the levator ani with the intact anal sphincter complex and its pudendal innervation
The coccygeus muscle
The obturator internus
The piriformis
questions.concept: The anorectal angle maintained by this sling is as important as the sphincter itself, which is why damage to it or to the nerve supply produces incontinence even when the sphincter ring appears intact.
questions.reference: Snell Clinical Anatomy by Regions 10e, Ch. The Pelvis and Perineum

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.topic: Skull base, cavernous sinus & meninges
questions.stem: Which structures pass through the jugular foramen, and what is the effect of a tumour there?
options: Cranial nerves IX, X and XI with the internal jugular vein, so a tumour causes loss of gag, hoarseness and weakness of trapezius and sternocleidomastoid
Cranial nerves III, IV and VI
The internal carotid artery and cranial nerve VII
Cranial nerve XII alone
questions.concept: This combination is Vernet syndrome, and involvement of the hypoglossal nerve in the nearby canal or of the sympathetic chain extends it to the other named jugular foramen syndromes.
questions.reference: Snell Clinical Anatomy by Regions 10e, Ch. The Head and Neck

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.topic: Skull base, cavernous sinus & meninges
questions.stem: Rupture of which vessel causes an extradural haematoma after a temporal skull fracture, and why does the patient deteriorate after a lucid interval?
options: The middle meningeal artery, because arterial bleeding gradually strips the dura from the skull until the expanding mass causes herniation
A bridging vein, because venous bleeding is slow
The cavernous sinus
The superior sagittal sinus
questions.concept: Because the dura is firmly adherent at the sutures the collection is limited and lens-shaped on imaging, and the lucid interval is the window in which surgical evacuation is life-saving.
questions.reference: Snell Clinical Anatomy by Regions 10e, Ch. The Head and Neck

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.topic: Skull base, cavernous sinus & meninges
questions.stem: Which anatomical relationship explains why an infection of the upper lip or nose can cause cavernous sinus thrombosis?
options: The facial vein communicates with the sinus through the superior ophthalmic vein and the deep facial vein, and these veins are valveless so flow can reverse
Infection spreads along the trigeminal nerve
Infection reaches it through the middle meningeal artery
Lymphatic drainage passes into the sinus
questions.concept: This valveless communication is the anatomical basis of the danger area of the face, and thrombosis presents with proptosis, chemosis, ophthalmoplegia and reduced corneal sensation.
questions.reference: Snell Clinical Anatomy by Regions 10e, Ch. The Head and Neck

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.topic: Thorax: lungs, pleura, diaphragm
questions.stem: At which site is an intercostal drain inserted for a pneumothorax, and which structures define the safe triangle?
options: The fifth intercostal space in the midaxillary line, within the triangle bounded by the lateral border of pectoralis major, the lateral border of latissimus dorsi and a line above the level of the nipple
The second space in the midclavicular line, below the nipple
The eighth space posteriorly
The subcostal margin anteriorly
questions.concept: Placing the drain within this triangle avoids the long thoracic nerve, the muscle bulk of the back and the diaphragm, and the tube is passed just above a rib to avoid the neurovascular bundle.
questions.reference: Snell Clinical Anatomy by Regions 10e, Ch. The Thorax

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.topic: Thorax: lungs, pleura, diaphragm
questions.stem: Which pleural recess is the most dependent part of the pleural cavity, and why does this matter for drainage?
options: The costodiaphragmatic recess, which is where a small effusion collects and where a needle is directed
The costomediastinal recess
The cupola of the pleura
The oblique fissure
questions.concept: The pleura extends about two ribs lower than the lung in this recess, so a needle placed there enters pleura without traversing lung, which is what makes thoracocentesis safe at that level.
questions.reference: Snell Clinical Anatomy by Regions 10e, Ch. The Thorax

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.topic: Thorax: lungs, pleura, diaphragm
questions.stem: Which anatomical feature of the diaphragm explains why a congenital diaphragmatic hernia is usually left-sided and posterolateral?
options: Failure of closure of the pleuroperitoneal canal at the foramen of Bochdalek, which closes later on the left and is protected on the right by the liver
Weakness at the foramen of Morgagni, which is posterolateral
A defect in the central tendon
Absence of the crura
questions.concept: Herniated bowel compresses the developing lung so pulmonary hypoplasia and pulmonary hypertension rather than the hernia itself determine survival, and a Morgagni hernia is instead anterior, retrosternal and usually right-sided.
questions.reference: Snell Clinical Anatomy by Regions 10e, Ch. The Thorax

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.topic: Upper limb: axilla, cubital fossa, hand spaces
questions.stem: Which nerve is at risk during axillary lymph node clearance, and what deficit results?
options: The long thoracic nerve, whose injury denervates serratus anterior and produces a winged scapula
The axillary nerve, producing deltoid paralysis
The musculocutaneous nerve, producing loss of elbow flexion
The radial nerve, producing wrist drop
questions.concept: The thoracodorsal nerve to latissimus dorsi is the other structure at risk, and both run on the walls of the axilla which is why they are identified and preserved during clearance.
questions.reference: Snell Clinical Anatomy by Regions 10e, Ch. The Upper Limb

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.topic: Upper limb: axilla, cubital fossa, hand spaces
questions.stem: Which tendon sheath arrangement explains why an infection of the little finger can spread to the forearm?
options: The digital sheath of the little finger is usually continuous with the ulnar bursa, which extends proximal to the flexor retinaculum into the space of Parona
Each digital sheath is entirely separate
The sheath communicates with the mid-palmar space directly
The sheath ends at the metacarpophalangeal joint
questions.concept: The thumb sheath similarly continues as the radial bursa, so infection in either of these two digits can reach the forearm whereas infection of the index, middle or ring finger is usually confined to the digit.
questions.reference: Snell Clinical Anatomy by Regions 10e, Ch. The Upper Limb

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.topic: Upper limb: axilla, cubital fossa, hand spaces
questions.stem: Which structure is compressed in the quadrangular space, and what is the resulting clinical picture?
options: The axillary nerve with the posterior circumflex humeral artery, causing deltoid weakness and sensory loss over the lateral shoulder
The radial nerve with the profunda brachii
The suprascapular nerve
The musculocutaneous nerve
questions.concept: The space is bounded by the humerus, the long head of triceps and the two teres muscles, and the same structures are injured by a surgical neck fracture or by inferior dislocation of the shoulder.
questions.reference: Snell Clinical Anatomy by Regions 10e, Ch. The Upper Limb
